name: Bayesian extraction of QGP transport coefficients
summary: Temperature-dependent eta/s and zeta/s are inferred by Bayesian calibration of hydrodynamic models against flow data, with Gaussian-process emulators and posterior uncertainty, the same parameter-estimation machinery used in cosmology.
breaks: Posteriors depend on the model family (initial state, freeze-out), so systematic model uncertainty can dominate.
sources: Heffernan et al. (2024). "Bayesian quantification of strongly interacting matter with color glass condensate initial conditions". *Phys. Rev. C* 109, 065207. [arXiv:2302.09478](https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.09478)

name: Bayesian multi-messenger inference of the dense-matter EOS
summary: The neutron-star EOS is inferred by Bayesian combination of chiral-EFT priors, heavy-pulsar masses, NICER pulse profiles and GW tidal deformabilities, using nonparametric (Gaussian-process, neural-network) EOS priors.
breaks: Prior choices at densities without data strongly shape posteriors on the maximum mass and quark-matter questions.
sources: Koehn et al. (2025). "From existing and new nuclear and astrophysical constraints to stringent limits on the equation of state of neutron-rich dense matter". *Phys. Rev. X* 15, 021014. [arXiv:2402.04172](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.04172)

name: Neutron-lifetime puzzle and combining discrepant data
summary: Beam (about 888 s) and bottle (about 878 s) neutron lifetimes disagree by about 4 sigma; PDG scale factors, Birge ratios and Bayesian treatments of unknown systematics are used to combine them, and the choice matters for BBN and |V_ud|.
breaks: Statistics cannot decide whether a systematic error or new physics (dark decay channels) causes the gap.
sources: González-Alonso, Naviliat-Cuncic & Severijns (2019). "New physics searches in nuclear and neutron β decay". *Prog. Part. Nucl. Phys.* 104, 165. [arXiv:1803.08732](https://arxiv.org/abs/1803.08732)

name: Bayesian EFT truncation errors for nuclear forces
summary: Chiral EFT predictions now carry theory error bars from Bayesian models of the omitted orders in Q/Lambda, treated as random coefficients with a learned scale, an EFT application of statistical inference.
map: y_k=y_{\rm ref}\sum_{n=0}^kc_nQ^n,\ \delta y_k\approx y_{\rm ref}\bar c\,\frac{Q^{k+1}}{\sqrt{1-Q^2}},\ c_n\sim\mathcal N(0,\bar c^2)
breaks: The assumption of natural, independent coefficients may fail when power counting is inconsistent.
sources: Furnstahl et al. (2015). "Quantifying truncation errors in effective field theory". *Phys. Rev. C* 92, 024005. [arXiv:1506.01343](https://arxiv.org/abs/1506.01343)

name: Radioactive decay as the model Poisson process
summary: Radioactive decay is the textbook Poisson process: counts have variance equal to the mean, intervals are exponential, and counting statistics, dead-time and background subtraction are the reference examples of uncertainty propagation.
breaks: Detector dead time and electronics make observed counts sub-Poissonian, and very short-lived sources violate stationarity.

name: Neutron and nuclear EDMs as tests of T and CP
summary: A permanent electric dipole moment of the neutron or a nucleus violates P and T; the neutron EDM bound underlies the strong CP problem, and octupole-deformed nuclei such as 225Ra enhance Schiff moments by orders of magnitude.
breaks: Converting EDM limits to CP-violating parameters needs nuclear and hadronic matrix elements with large uncertainties.
sources: Abel et al. (2020). "Measurement of the Permanent Electric Dipole Moment of the Neutron". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 124, 081803. [arXiv:2001.11966](https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.11966)

name: Parity violation in nuclear beta decay
summary: Wu's 1957 measurement of the electron asymmetry from polarized 60Co showed the weak interaction maximally violates parity, establishing the V-A structure of beta decay.
sources: Wu et al. (1957). "Experimental Test of Parity Conservation in Beta Decay". *Phys. Rev.* 105, 1413. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.105.1413](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.105.1413)

name: Isospin and Wigner SU(4) symmetry of nuclear forces
summary: Charge independence of nuclear forces makes isospin an SU(2) symmetry with protons and neutrons as a doublet; Wigner's combined spin-isospin SU(4) supermultiplets explain why light-nucleus binding and Gamow-Teller patterns follow the 4-fold degeneracy.
breaks: Isospin is broken by Coulomb forces and the u-d quark mass difference (~1 percent), and SU(4) is broken strongly by spin-orbit forces in heavier nuclei.
sources: Heisenberg (1932). "Über den Bau der Atomkerne. I". *Z. Phys.* 77, 1. [doi:10.1007/BF01342433](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01342433)

Wigner (1937). "On the Consequences of the Symmetry of the Nuclear Hamiltonian on the Spectroscopy of Nuclei". *Phys. Rev.* 51, 106. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.51.106](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.51.106)

name: Elliott SU(3) and interacting-boson dynamical symmetries
summary: Collective rotation emerges from the shell model through Elliott's SU(3) for the harmonic oscillator, and the interacting boson model's U(6) group chains U(5), SU(3) and O(6) give the vibrational, rotational and gamma-soft limits of nuclear spectra.
breaks: Real nuclei lie between limits and spin-orbit coupling breaks Elliott SU(3) beyond the sd shell (pseudo- and quasi-SU(3) partly restore it).
sources: Elliott (1958). "Collective motion in the nuclear shell model. I. Classification schemes for states of mixed configuration". *Proc. R. Soc. A* 245, 128. [doi:10.1098/rspa.1958.0072](https://doi.org/10.1098/rspa.1958.0072)

Arima & Iachello (1976). "Interacting boson model of collective states I. The vibrational limit". *Ann. Phys.* 99, 253. [doi:10.1016/0003-4916(76)90097-x](https://doi.org/10.1016/0003-4916(76)90097-x)

name: Seniority and quasispin: pairing as an SU(2) algebra
summary: Racah's seniority scheme and Kerman's quasispin show that pair creation and annihilation in a j-shell close an SU(2) algebra, which makes the pairing Hamiltonian exactly solvable and explains constant 2+ energies in semi-magic nuclei.
breaks: Seniority is exact only in a single j-shell or with degenerate orbits; multi-j shells and quadrupole forces mix seniorities.
sources: Racah (1943). "Theory of Complex Spectra. III". *Phys. Rev.* 63, 367. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.63.367](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.63.367)

name: Conserved vector current and superallowed ft values
summary: The vector weak current is the Noether current of isospin (CVC), so Fermi matrix elements of superallowed 0+ to 0+ decays are fixed by symmetry; after small isospin-breaking and radiative corrections all ft values agree, which tests CVC and gives |V_ud|.
breaks: Isospin-breaking corrections delta_C are model-dependent and are the leading theory uncertainty.
sources: Feynman & Gell-Mann (1958). "Theory of the Fermi Interaction". *Phys. Rev.* 109, 193. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.109.193](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.109.193)

Hardy & Towner (2020). "Superallowed 0+→0+ nuclear β decays: 2020 critical survey, with implications for Vud and CKM unitarity". *Phys. Rev. C* 102, 045501. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevC.102.045501](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevC.102.045501)

name: Chiral restoration and O(4) universality
summary: The QCD transition is chiral-symmetry restoration; Pisarski and Wilczek argued that for two massless flavours it falls in the 3D O(4) universality class, and lattice data at physical masses show a crossover with O(4) scaling remnants.
breaks: Explicit quark masses turn the transition into a crossover, and the U(1)_A anomaly strength affects the universality class.
sources: Pisarski & Wilczek (1984). "Remarks on the chiral phase transition in chromodynamics". *Phys. Rev. D* 29, 338. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevD.29.338](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevD.29.338)

name: Pions as Goldstone bosons organize nuclear forces
summary: Spontaneous breaking of QCD's chiral SU(2)xSU(2) symmetry makes pions light pseudo-Goldstone bosons with derivative couplings; this fixes one-pion exchange as the long-range nuclear force and Weinberg's power counting in Q/Lambda_chi.
map: SU(2)_L\times SU(2)_R\to SU(2)_V;\ m_\pi^2f_\pi^2=-(m_u+m_d)\langle\bar qq\rangle;\ V_{1\pi}\propto\frac{g_A^2}{f_\pi^2}\frac{(\sigma_1\cdot q)(\sigma_2\cdot q)}{q^2+m_\pi^2}
breaks: Nonperturbative NN binding forces iteration of the potential, and power-counting consistency in that regime is debated.
sources: Weinberg (1990). "Nuclear forces from chiral lagrangians". *Phys. Lett. B* 251, 288. [doi:10.1016/0370-2693(90)90938-3](https://doi.org/10.1016/0370-2693(90)90938-3)
Epelbaum, Hammer & Meißner (2009). "Modern theory of nuclear forces". *Rev. Mod. Phys.* 81, 1773. [arXiv:0811.1338](https://arxiv.org/abs/0811.1338)

name: Nuclear deformation and pairing as broken symmetries
summary: Deformed mean fields break rotational symmetry and BCS pairing breaks particle number; in finite nuclei the broken symmetry shows up as rotational bands (Anderson-tower rotations) and pairing rotations, restored by projection.
map: E_J=\frac{\hbar^2}{2\mathcal I}J(J+1)\ \text{(rotational tower)};\ E_{\rm pair\ rot}\propto\frac{(N-N_0)^2}{2\mathcal I_{\rm pair}}
breaks: A finite system cannot truly break a continuous symmetry; the 'Goldstone modes' are discrete rotational excitations whose spacing shrinks only as A grows.
sources: Bender, Heenen & Reinhard (2003). "Self-consistent mean-field models for nuclear structure". *Rev. Mod. Phys.* 75, 121. [doi:10.1103/RevModPhys.75.121](https://doi.org/10.1103/RevModPhys.75.121)

name: Taylor's blast-wave estimate of a fission yield
summary: G. I. Taylor estimated the energy of the first atomic explosion from photographs of the fireball radius versus time using only dimensional analysis, the classic Taylor-Sedov scaling.
breaks: Scaling fixes the yield only up to the dimensionless constant C(gamma), which needs a similarity solution.
sources: Taylor (1950). "The formation of a blast wave by a very intense explosion II. The atomic explosion of 1945". *Proc. R. Soc. A* 201, 175. [doi:10.1098/rspa.1950.0050](https://doi.org/10.1098/rspa.1950.0050)

name: Oklo natural reactor bounds varying constants
summary: The 2-billion-year-old Oklo natural fission reactor depleted 149Sm through its 0.1 eV neutron resonance; the resonance position today matches, bounding changes of the fine-structure constant to about 1e-7 over that time.
breaks: The bound depends on modelling the reactor's neutron spectrum and temperature and on assuming only alpha varies.
sources: Shlyakhter (1976). "Direct test of the constancy of fundamental nuclear constants". *Nature* 264, 340. [doi:10.1038/264340a0](https://doi.org/10.1038/264340a0)

name: Proton radius and the Rydberg constant in CODATA
summary: The proton charge radius enters hydrogen energy levels, so it is adjusted jointly with the Rydberg constant; the muonic-hydrogen radius (0.84 fm) shifted the CODATA values of both after the proton-radius puzzle.
breaks: Electron-scattering extractions depend on form-factor fit extrapolation to Q^2 = 0.
sources: Pohl et al. (2010). "The size of the proton". *Nature* 466, 213. [doi:10.1038/nature09250](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature09250)

Tiesinga et al. (2021). "CODATA recommended values of the fundamental physical constants: 2018". *Rev. Mod. Phys.* 93, 025010. [doi:10.1103/RevModPhys.93.025010](https://doi.org/10.1103/RevModPhys.93.025010)

name: BBN constrains variation of constants
summary: Primordial helium and deuterium are sensitive to the neutron-proton mass difference, deuteron binding, G_F and G at T ~ 1 MeV, so BBN bounds variations of the fine-structure constant, quark masses and Newton's constant over 13.8 Gyr.
breaks: Correlated variations in unified theories make single-constant bounds model-dependent.
sources: Iocco et al. (2009). "Primordial Nucleosynthesis: from precision cosmology to fundamental physics". *Phys. Rep.* 472, 1. [arXiv:0809.0631](https://arxiv.org/abs/0809.0631)

name: Thorium-229 nuclear clock and variation of alpha
summary: The 8.4 eV 229Th isomer energy results from near-cancellation of MeV-scale Coulomb and nuclear energies, so a nuclear clock is predicted to be orders of magnitude more sensitive to drifts of the fine-structure constant and quark masses than atomic clocks.
breaks: The enhancement factor depends on the difference of Coulomb energies of two nuclear states, which is uncertain to a factor of a few.
sources: Flambaum (2006). "Enhanced Effect of Temporal Variation of the Fine Structure Constant and the Strong Interaction in 229Th". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 97, 092502. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.97.092502](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.97.092502)

name: Atomic masses, the mole and the 2019 SI
summary: Nuclear masses are measured as ratios to 12C (the unified atomic mass unit); Penning-trap mass ratios feed CODATA, and the 28Si-sphere Avogadro determination behind the new kilogram relied on isotopic enrichment and neutron-activation impurity analysis.
breaks: Since 2019 the mole is defined by a fixed N_A, so m_u is no longer exactly 1 g/mol divided by N_A.
sources: Wang et al. (2021). "The AME 2020 atomic mass evaluation (II). Tables, graphs and references". *Chinese Phys. C* 45, 030003. [doi:10.1088/1674-1137/abddaf](https://doi.org/10.1088/1674-1137/abddaf)

name: DFT as computational physics' largest application
summary: Kohn-Sham DFT with plane waves, pseudopotentials, FFTs and iterative eigensolvers is among the most heavily used computational methods in all of science; numerical analysis (basis convergence, k-point sampling, self-consistency mixing) controls its accuracy.
sources: Kresse & Furthmüller (1996). "Efficiency of ab-initio total energy calculations for metals and semiconductors using a plane-wave basis set". *Comput. Mater. Sci.* 6, 15. [doi:10.1016/0927-0256(96)00008-0](https://doi.org/10.1016/0927-0256(96)00008-0)

name: Machine-learned interatomic potentials trained on DFT
summary: Neural-network and kernel potentials fitted to DFT energies and forces reach near-DFT accuracy at the cost of classical force fields, enabling million-atom, nanosecond simulations of phase transitions, defects and hydrides.
sources: Behler & Parrinello (2007). "Generalized Neural-Network Representation of High-Dimensional Potential-Energy Surfaces". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 98, 146401. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.98.146401](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.98.146401)

name: Machine-learned structure predicts glassy dynamics
summary: A machine-learned structural order parameter ('softness') trained on local particle environments predicts which particles in a supercooled liquid will rearrange, connecting hidden structure to dynamical heterogeneity.
sources: Schoenholz et al. (2016). "A structural approach to relaxation in glassy liquids". *Nat. Phys.* 12, 469. [arXiv:1506.07772](https://arxiv.org/abs/1506.07772)

name: Neural-network quantum states
summary: Neural networks used as variational wavefunctions (restricted Boltzmann machines, then transformers) are optimized by variational Monte Carlo and now compete with DMRG and QMC on frustrated magnets and the doped Hubbard model.
sources: Carleo & Troyer (2017). "Solving the quantum many-body problem with artificial neural networks". *Science* 355, 602. [arXiv:1606.02318](https://arxiv.org/abs/1606.02318)

name: Ab initio molecular dynamics
summary: Car-Parrinello and Born-Oppenheimer molecular dynamics integrate nuclear motion on DFT forces computed on the fly, unifying electronic structure with MD for liquids, melting and high-pressure phases.
sources: Car & Parrinello (1985). "Unified Approach for Molecular Dynamics and Density-Functional Theory". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 55, 2471. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.55.2471](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.55.2471)

name: Molecular dynamics of supercooled liquids and jamming
summary: Simulations of Lennard-Jones and soft-sphere mixtures supply dynamical heterogeneity, the Kauzmann and mode-coupling tests and jamming criticality, but are limited to ~microsecond times, about 10^-6 of the laboratory glass-transition timescale.
sources: Debenedetti & Stillinger (2001). "Supercooled liquids and the glass transition". *Nature* 410, 259. [doi:10.1038/35065704](https://doi.org/10.1038/35065704)

name: Bead-spring simulations of entangled polymers
summary: The Kremer-Grest bead-spring model showed by MD the crossover from Rouse to reptation dynamics in entangled melts and remains the standard coarse-grained test bed for polymer rheology.
sources: Kremer & Grest (1990). "Dynamics of entangled linear polymer melts: A molecular-dynamics simulation". *J. Chem. Phys.* 92, 5057. [doi:10.1063/1.458541](https://doi.org/10.1063/1.458541)

name: Cluster Monte Carlo for magnetic spin models
summary: Critical slowing down in Metropolis simulations of Ising and Heisenberg magnets was beaten by Swendsen-Wang and Wolff cluster updates built on the Fortuin-Kasteleyn mapping; loop and worm algorithms extend this to quantum magnets.
sources: Swendsen & Wang (1987). "Nonuniversal critical dynamics in Monte Carlo simulations". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 58, 86. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.58.86](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.58.86)

name: Quantum Monte Carlo and the fermion sign problem
summary: Determinant, auxiliary-field and diagrammatic QMC map correlated electrons onto Monte Carlo sampling in imaginary time; for doped fermions and frustrated magnets the weights turn negative and the sign problem makes cost exponential.
sources: Troyer & Wiese (2005). "Computational Complexity and Fundamental Limitations to Fermionic Quantum Monte Carlo Simulations". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 94, 170201. [arXiv:cond-mat/0408370](https://arxiv.org/abs/cond-mat/0408370)

name: Entanglement structure of correlated ground states
summary: Area-law entanglement in gapped correlated phases is what makes tensor-network compression possible; deviations (log corrections at criticality, topological entanglement entropy) diagnose the phase.

name: Topological order as an entanglement pattern
summary: Topological order shows up as a constant negative correction to area-law entanglement, the topological entanglement entropy gamma=ln D, and string-net and toric-code ground states are exact PEPS with virtual symmetries; tensor networks thereby identify topological phases numerically.
sources: Levin & Wen (2006). "Detecting Topological Order in a Ground State Wave Function". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 96, 110405. [arXiv:cond-mat/0510613](https://arxiv.org/abs/cond-mat/0510613)

name: DMRG and tensor networks for correlated electrons
summary: DMRG, invented for quantum spin chains, is a variational method over matrix product states; PEPS, MERA and their 2D cylinder implementations now give benchmark ground states of Hubbard and frustrated spin models, limited by area-law entanglement growth.
sources: Schollwoeck (2011). "The density-matrix renormalization group in the age of matrix product states". *Ann. Phys.* 326, 96. [arXiv:1008.3477](https://arxiv.org/abs/1008.3477)

name: MERA and entanglement at quantum critical points
summary: Critical ground states violate the area law logarithmically; the multiscale entanglement renormalization ansatz (MERA) captures this with a scale-invariant tensor network that implements real-space RG and resembles a discretized AdS geometry.
map: S(\ell)=\frac c3\ln\frac\ell a\ (\text{1+1D CFT});\ \text{MERA layers}\leftrightarrow\text{RG scale}\leftrightarrow\text{radial AdS coordinate}
sources: Vidal (2008). "Class of Quantum Many-Body States That Can Be Efficiently Simulated". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 101, 110501. [arXiv:quant-ph/0610099](https://arxiv.org/abs/quant-ph/0610099)
Swingle (2012). "Entanglement Renormalization and Holography". *Phys. Rev. D* 86, 065007. [arXiv:0905.1317](https://arxiv.org/abs/0905.1317)

name: Emergence and the limits of reductionism
summary: Anderson's 'More is different' and Laughlin and Pines' 'Theory of Everything' used broken symmetry, quasiparticles and protected quantization in correlated matter as the central examples in the philosophical debate over emergence and reduction.
sources: Anderson (1972). "More Is Different". *Science* 177, 393. [doi:10.1126/science.177.4047.393](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.177.4047.393)
Laughlin & Pines (2000). "The Theory of Everything". *Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci.* 97, 28. [doi:10.1073/pnas.97.1.28](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.97.1.28)

name: Kramers-Kronig relations for lattice and optical response
summary: Causality makes the dielectric and phonon response functions analytic in the upper half-plane, so absorption and dispersion are Hilbert transforms of each other; this links the TO-phonon resonance, reflectivity and the Lyddane-Sachs-Teller relation.

name: Bloch theorem as Floquet theory of periodic ODEs
summary: Bloch's theorem is Floquet's 1883 theorem for linear differential equations with periodic coefficients; bands and gaps of the Kronig-Penney and nearly-free-electron models are the stability and instability zones of Hill's and Mathieu's equations.

name: Many-body Green's functions and DMFT
summary: Correlated-electron theory is built on Matsubara Green's functions and self-energies; DMFT maps the lattice problem onto an impurity whose local Green's function is fixed self-consistently, an operational use of Dyson's equation.
sources: Georges, Kotliar, Krauth & Rozenberg (1996). "Dynamical mean-field theory of strongly correlated fermion systems and the limit of infinite dimensions". *Rev. Mod. Phys.* 68, 13. [doi:10.1103/RevModPhys.68.13](https://doi.org/10.1103/RevModPhys.68.13)

name: Bloch bands as an eigenvalue problem
summary: Band structure is the spectral decomposition of a lattice-translation-invariant Hamiltonian: Bloch's theorem block-diagonalizes it by crystal momentum, leaving finite Hermitian matrices H(k) to diagonalize.
map: [H,T_{\mathbf R}]=0\Rightarrow H=\bigoplus_{\mathbf k}H(\mathbf k),\ H(\mathbf k)u_{n\mathbf k}=E_n(\mathbf k)u_{n\mathbf k}

name: Berry curvature as the curvature of a bundle
summary: Berry connection and curvature are a U(1) connection and its curvature on the bundle of Bloch states over the Brillouin-zone torus; the Chern number is the first Chern class and the quantum geometric tensor combines a metric with this curvature.
map:
\mathcal A=i\langle u|duangle,\ \Omega=d\mathcal A,\ C= rac1{2\pi}\int_{T^2}\Omega\in\mathbb Z;\ Q_{\mu
u}=g_{\mu
u}-	frac i2\Omega_{\mu
u}
sources: Simon (1983). "Holonomy, the Quantum Adiabatic Theorem, and Berry's Phase". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 51, 2167. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.51.2167](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.51.2167)

Thouless, Kohmoto, Nightingale & den Nijs (1982). "Quantized Hall Conductance in a Two-Dimensional Periodic Potential". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 49, 405. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.49.405](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.49.405)

name: Shot noise and Johnson noise in conductors
summary: The Johnson-Nyquist and Schottky formulas of instrumentation are limits of mesoscopic noise theory: shot noise reduced by the Fano factor sum T(1-T)/sum T, and measuring it revealed the e/3 charge of fractional quantum Hall quasiparticles.
sources: Blanter & Büttiker (2000). "Shot noise in mesoscopic conductors". *Phys. Rep.* 336, 1. [arXiv:cond-mat/9910158](https://arxiv.org/abs/cond-mat/9910158)
de-Picciotto et al. (1997). "Direct observation of a fractional charge". *Nature* 389, 162. [arXiv:cond-mat/9707289](https://arxiv.org/abs/cond-mat/9707289)

name: Superconducting cryogenic sensors
summary: Transition-edge sensors, kinetic-inductance detectors and superconducting nanowire single-photon detectors turn the superconducting transition and the small gap into energy-resolving, photon-counting sensors for X-ray, optical and millimetre-wave astronomy and quantum optics.
sources: Irwin (1995). "An application of electrothermal feedback for high resolution cryogenic particle detection". *Appl. Phys. Lett.* 66, 1998. [doi:10.1063/1.113674](https://doi.org/10.1063/1.113674)
Day et al. (2003). "A broadband superconducting detector suitable for use in large arrays". *Nature* 425, 817. [doi:10.1038/nature02037](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature02037)

name: SQUIDs as instrumentation
summary: SQUIDs are the most sensitive magnetic-flux detectors and the readout amplifiers of cryogenic sensor arrays; their noise is set by Josephson-junction physics and can approach the quantum limit.

name: Space groups and representations in crystals
summary: The 230 space groups and their irreducible representations label Bloch bands, phonon branches and selection rules, explain systematic absences in diffraction, and the crystallographic restriction (no 5-fold axes) made quasicrystals a surprise.
map: \{R|\mathbf t\}\psi_{n\mathbf k}=\psi_{n,R\mathbf k};\ \text{little group }G_{\mathbf k}\ \text{irreps label bands};\ 2\cos(2\pi/n)\in\mathbb Z
sources: Shechtman et al. (1984). "Metallic Phase with Long-Range Orientational Order and No Translational Symmetry". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 53, 1951. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.53.1951](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.53.1951)

name: Topological order as broken higher-form symmetry
summary: Generalized (higher-form) global symmetries act on line and surface operators; deconfined topological phases such as the toric code spontaneously break a 1-form symmetry, extending the symmetry-breaking classification of phases to topological order and its mixed-state versions.
sources: Gaiotto, Kapustin, Seiberg & Willett (2015). "Generalized Global Symmetries". *J. High Energy Phys.* 02, 172. [arXiv:1412.5148](https://arxiv.org/abs/1412.5148)

name: Topological quantum chemistry via band representations
summary: Induced (band) representations of space groups decide whether a set of bands can come from localized symmetric Wannier orbitals; when they cannot, the bands are topological, which turned representation theory into a high-throughput topology classifier.
sources: Bradlyn et al. (2017). "Topological quantum chemistry". *Nature* 547, 298. [arXiv:1703.02050](https://arxiv.org/abs/1703.02050)

name: Altermagnets break time reversal without magnetization
summary: Altermagnets lift Kramers spin degeneracy by breaking the combined time-reversal-plus-translation symmetry of ordinary antiferromagnets while keeping zero net moment, so T-odd responses (anomalous Hall, spin splitting) appear without stray fields.
sources: Krempaský et al. (2024). "Altermagnetic lifting of Kramers spin degeneracy". *Nature* 626, 517. [doi:10.1038/s41586-023-06907-7](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-023-06907-7)

name: The tenfold way from T, C and chiral symmetry
summary: Gapped free-fermion phases fall into ten Altland-Zirnbauer classes set by whether time reversal T, particle-hole C and chiral S symmetries are present and square to +1 or -1; with dimension this gives the periodic table of topological insulators and superconductors.
sources: Altland & Zirnbauer (1997). "Nonstandard symmetry classes in mesoscopic normal-superconducting hybrid structures". *Phys. Rev. B* 55, 1142. [arXiv:cond-mat/9602137](https://arxiv.org/abs/cond-mat/9602137)
Kitaev (2009). "Periodic table for topological insulators and superconductors". *AIP Conf. Proc.* 1134, 22. [arXiv:0901.2686](https://arxiv.org/abs/0901.2686)

name: Kramers pairs protect topological insulators
summary: The antiunitary time-reversal operator with Theta^2=-1 forces Kramers degeneracy at time-reversal-invariant momenta, giving the Z2 invariant and protecting the surface Dirac cone against non-magnetic backscattering.
sources: Kane & Mele (2005). "Z2 Topological Order and the Quantum Spin Hall Effect". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 95, 146802. [arXiv:cond-mat/0506581](https://arxiv.org/abs/cond-mat/0506581)

name: Spin-group symmetry classification of altermagnets
summary: Altermagnets are defined by spin-group symmetry, in which spin and lattice operations act independently when spin-orbit coupling is negligible; opposite-spin sublattices related by a rotation rather than a translation or inversion give d-, g- or i-wave spin splitting.
map: [C_2\|C_{4z}]\ \text{(spin flip }\otimes\text{ lattice rotation)}\Rightarrow E_\uparrow(\mathbf k)-E_\downarrow(\mathbf k)\propto k_xk_y
sources: Šmejkal, Sinova & Jungwirth (2022). "Emerging Research Landscape of Altermagnetism". *Phys. Rev. X* 12, 040501. [arXiv:2204.10844](https://arxiv.org/abs/2204.10844)

name: Chiral anomaly breaks a Noether current in Weyl semimetals
summary: The axial charge of Weyl fermions is conserved classically by Noether's theorem but not quantum mechanically: parallel E and B pump electrons between Weyl nodes of opposite chirality at the Adler-Bell-Jackiw rate, seen as negative longitudinal magnetoresistance.
sources: Nielsen & Ninomiya (1983). "The Adler-Bell-Jackiw anomaly and Weyl fermions in a crystal". *Phys. Lett. B* 130, 389. [doi:10.1016/0370-2693(83)91529-0](https://doi.org/10.1016/0370-2693(83)91529-0)

name: Magnons as Goldstone bosons and their counting
summary: Magnons are the Goldstone modes of broken spin-rotation symmetry: antiferromagnets have two linearly dispersing type-A modes, while ferromagnets have one quadratic type-B mode because the broken generators have a non-zero commutator expectation; Mermin-Wagner forbids such order in 2D at T>0.
sources: Watanabe & Murayama (2012). "Unified Description of Nambu-Goldstone Bosons without Lorentz Invariance". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 108, 251602. [arXiv:1203.0609](https://arxiv.org/abs/1203.0609)

Mermin & Wagner (1966). "Absence of Ferromagnetism or Antiferromagnetism in One- or Two-Dimensional Isotropic Heisenberg Models". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 17, 1133. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.17.1133](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.17.1133)

name: Spin liquids: order without symmetry breaking
summary: Quantum spin liquids are the main counterexample to the Landau paradigm: frustration prevents spontaneous symmetry breaking down to T=0, and the low-energy theory instead has emergent gauge fields and fractionalized spinons, so the phase is classified by topology rather than an order parameter.
map: f=|\theta_{CW}|/T_N\gg1;\ \text{no local }\langle\mathbf S_i\rangle\neq0,\ \text{emergent }\mathbb Z_2\text{ or U(1) gauge field}
sources: Balents (2010). "Spin liquids in frustrated magnets". *Nature* 464, 199. [doi:10.1038/nature08917](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature08917)

name: Nematic order, Goldstone modes and homotopy of defects
summary: A nematic breaks rotational symmetry with order-parameter space RP^2; its director fluctuations are Goldstone modes and its defects are classified by homotopy groups, pi_1(RP^2)=Z_2 allowing half-integer disclinations, which is the general topological theory of defects in ordered media.
sources: Mermin (1979). "The topological theory of defects in ordered media". *Rev. Mod. Phys.* 51, 591. [doi:10.1103/RevModPhys.51.591](https://doi.org/10.1103/RevModPhys.51.591)

name: Superconductivity as broken U(1) gauge symmetry
summary: A superconductor is the condensed-matter Higgs phase: a charged condensate with a phase that breaks U(1), whose would-be Goldstone mode is eaten by the photon, giving the Meissner effect and flux quantization.
sources: Anderson (1963). "Plasmons, Gauge Invariance, and Mass". *Phys. Rev.* 130, 439. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.130.439](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.130.439)

name: Ginzburg-Landau theory is the abelian Higgs model
summary: The Ginzburg-Landau free energy of a superconductor is, term by term, the static abelian Higgs Lagrangian; the coherence length and penetration depth are the inverse Higgs and photon masses, and kappa=lambda/xi separates type I from type II exactly where Nielsen-Olesen strings attract or repel.
sources: Anderson (1963). "Plasmons, Gauge Invariance, and Mass". *Phys. Rev.* 130, 439. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.130.439](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.130.439)

name: Scaling arguments in polymer physics
summary: Flory's free-energy balance and de Gennes' blob scaling derive polymer size, osmotic pressure and dynamics from dimensional analysis plus a single exponent, a showcase of scaling reasoning without solving the full model.
sources: Flory (1949). "The Configuration of Real Polymer Chains". *J. Chem. Phys.* 17, 303. [doi:10.1063/1.1747243](https://doi.org/10.1063/1.1747243)

name: Planckian time from dimensional analysis
summary: At a quantum critical point the only energy scale is temperature, so dimensional analysis gives a relaxation time hbar/k_BT; strange metals saturate this Planckian bound, with measured scattering rates hbar/tau~alpha k_BT and alpha~1.
sources: Zaanen (2004). "Why the temperature is high". *Nature* 430, 512. [doi:10.1038/430512a](https://doi.org/10.1038/430512a)

name: Quantum Hall effect measures the fine-structure constant
summary: von Klitzing introduced the quantized Hall resistance as a determination of alpha, since R_K=h/e^2=mu_0 c/(2 alpha); QHE data entered CODATA adjustments of alpha before the 2019 SI made R_K exact.
sources: von Klitzing, Dorda & Pepper (1980). "New Method for High-Accuracy Determination of the Fine-Structure Constant Based on Quantized Hall Resistance". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 45, 494. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.45.494](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.45.494)

name: Graphene quantum Hall resistance standards
summary: Epitaxial graphene on SiC shows wide, robust nu=2 plateaus at higher temperature and lower field than GaAs, allowing table-top quantum resistance standards with part-per-billion accuracy.
sources: Tzalenchuk et al. (2010). "Towards a quantum resistance standard based on epitaxial graphene". *Nat. Nanotechnol.* 5, 186. [arXiv:0909.1220](https://arxiv.org/abs/0909.1220)

name: Single-electron pumps and the quantum ampere
summary: Coulomb-blockaded quantum dots and metallic islands clocked at frequency f transfer exactly one electron per cycle, realizing I=ef directly from the fixed elementary charge and closing the quantum metrology triangle with Josephson and quantum Hall standards.
sources: Pekola et al. (2013). "Single-electron current sources: Toward a refined definition of the ampere". *Rev. Mod. Phys.* 85, 1421. [arXiv:1208.4030](https://arxiv.org/abs/1208.4030)

name: Josephson voltage standard and the 2019 SI
summary: The AC Josephson effect fixes voltage to frequency through K_J=2e/h exactly; with e and h fixed in the 2019 SI, Josephson arrays realize the volt and, with the Kibble balance, the kilogram.
sources: Josephson (1962). "Possible new effects in superconductive tunnelling". *Phys. Lett.* 1, 251. [doi:10.1016/0031-9163(62)91369-0](https://doi.org/10.1016/0031-9163(62)91369-0)

name: Quantum Hall resistance standard
summary: Hall plateaus at R_xy=h/(nu e^2) independent of material and geometry realize the ohm via the von Klitzing constant R_K=h/e^2, exact in the 2019 SI.
sources: von Klitzing, Dorda & Pepper (1980). "New Method for High-Accuracy Determination of the Fine-Structure Constant Based on Quantized Hall Resistance". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 45, 494. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.45.494](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.45.494)

name: Simulation-based inference and emulators for LSS
summary: Neural emulators replace expensive N-body or Boltzmann runs, and neural density estimators enable likelihood-free inference from galaxy surveys and weak lensing.

name: ML classification of transients
summary: Time-domain surveys such as ZTF and Rubin rely on neural classifiers and anomaly detection to triage millions of alerts and photometrically classify supernovae.

name: N-body simulations as gravitational MD
summary: Cosmological N-body codes use the same symplectic leapfrog integrators and force softening as MD, with tree or particle-mesh gravity in place of Lennard-Jones forces.

name: MCMC for CMB parameter estimation
summary: Metropolis-Hastings sampling, as in CosmoMC, explores the multidimensional CMB likelihood. It made six-parameter ΛCDM fits to Planck tractable.

name: Boltzmann codes for CMB spectra
summary: CAMB and CLASS integrate coupled Einstein–Boltzmann hierarchies for photons, baryons, neutrinos and dark matter. Stiff ODE solvers handle tight coupling before recombination.

name: Hydrodynamic solvers in cosmological simulations
summary: Finite-volume, AMR and SPH schemes evolve gas with gravity in galaxy-formation simulations. Subgrid models for cooling, star formation and feedback supply the physics that is not resolved.

name: Symplectic integrators for orbital dynamics
summary: Wisdom–Holman mapping splits the Hamiltonian into Kepler and perturbation parts. It enabled long-term chaos studies of planetary orbits and the Nice model.

name: Dark matter vs modified gravity as theory choice
summary: The MOND versus particle dark matter debate mirrors Neptune versus Vulcan: anomalies can be absorbed by new matter or new laws. It engages Lakatosian research programmes and underdetermination.
breaks: Unlike Vulcan, the dark-matter hypothesis has independent evidence from the CMB and the Bullet Cluster, and MOND struggles with clusters.

name: Spherical harmonics and Legendre expansion of the CMB
summary: The temperature sky is expanded in spherical harmonics, and the angular power spectrum is the rotation-invariant variance. Statistical isotropy makes the C_ℓ the full description of Gaussian fluctuations.
map: \frac{\delta T}{T}=\sum a_{\ell m}Y_{\ell m},\ C_\ell=\langle|a_{\ell m}|^2\rangle

name: Special functions in galactic potentials
summary: Galactic potentials and Poisson solutions in disk geometry use Bessel functions, Legendre expansions and elliptic integrals. They underpin mass models fitted to Gaia kinematics.

name: Poisson equation and the growth of perturbations
summary: Linear perturbations obey a damped-oscillator-like ODE sourced by the Poisson equation. Green's-function solutions yield growth factors and the transfer function that shapes the matter power spectrum.

name: Stellar structure as a nonlinear boundary-value problem
summary: Hydrostatic equilibrium, mass continuity, energy generation and transport form coupled ODEs with boundary conditions at centre and surface. The Lane–Emden equation is the polytropic special case.

name: FLRW as a maximally symmetric spacetime
summary: The FLRW metric is the warped product of time with a maximally symmetric 3-space of constant curvature k. Friedmann equations follow from the Einstein tensor evaluated on it.

name: Lensing as geodesic deflection in curved spacetime
summary: Null geodesics in a weak-field metric give the deflection angle, and the lens equation maps it to image positions. Shear and convergence are components of the Jacobian of the lens map.

name: TES bolometers and CMB polarimetry
summary: CMB experiments such as ACT, SPT and BICEP use transition-edge-sensor arrays limited by photon and thermal noise, with SQUID multiplexed readout.

name: Cryogenic sensors and low-background detectors
summary: Transition-edge sensors, bolometers and low-noise readout, developed for general detector physics, enable sub-GeV dark-matter searches. Noise floors and background rejection set the reach.

name: Cosmology as statistical inference
summary: Cosmology has a single observable universe, so cosmic variance, MCMC chains, Fisher forecasts and Bayesian evidence are the core tools for extracting parameters and testing models.

name: Bayesian inference of ΛCDM parameters
summary: Cosmological parameters are fitted by Bayesian posterior sampling over likelihoods built from CMB, BAO and supernova data, with priors and model comparison deciding between ΛCDM extensions.

name: Priors, degeneracies and model selection in ΛCDM
summary: Parameter degeneracies (e.g. Ωm–H0, w0–wa) and prior choices shape cosmological constraints. Information criteria and Bayes factors adjudicate extensions such as curvature or dynamical dark energy.

name: Profile likelihood and exclusion limits
summary: Direct-detection limits use profile-likelihood tests, CLs and the Feldman–Cousins construction. Background-dominated searches face the look-elsewhere effect and the neutrino fog.

name: Detection statistics for exoplanet signals
summary: Planet detection uses periodograms, false-alarm probabilities, MCMC orbit fits and Bayesian model comparison for the number of planets. Noise from stellar activity requires Gaussian-process modelling.

name: Systematics budgets in the H0 tension
summary: The H0 tension's significance depends on how statistical and systematic errors, covariances and calibration chains (Cepheids, TRGB) are propagated. Distance-ladder error budgets are an applied GUM-style case.

name: CP violation and the baryon asymmetry
summary: Sakharov's conditions require C and CP violation, baryon-number violation and departure from equilibrium to generate the matter–antimatter asymmetry. The Standard Model's CP violation is far too small.

name: Particle-physics symmetries behind annihilation signals
summary: Annihilation channels and spectra depend on the gauge representation and quantum numbers of the dark-matter candidate, as for a WIMP in SU(2)_L multiplets. These fix branching fractions to gamma rays and antimatter.

name: Broken time translation and energy in an expanding universe
summary: FLRW has no timelike Killing vector, so total energy is not conserved. Radiation redshifts as a⁻⁴ and the cosmological constant does work, though local ∇_μT^{μν}=0 persists.
breaks: Only the global energy notion fails; local covariant conservation holds.

name: Solar oscillations as normal modes
summary: Helioseismic p-modes are standing waves of the solar cavity, described by spherical-harmonic eigenfunctions. Frequencies invert to give the sound-speed profile, as in a spectral problem for an oscillator.
breaks: The Sun is a non-ideal, rotating, convective cavity, so modes are damped and stochastically excited, and rotation splits the degenerate m levels.

name: Inflaton as an order parameter
summary: A scalar field rolling in a potential mirrors the order parameter of a symmetry-breaking transition. The same potential structure underlies Higgs-like phase transitions, topological defects and old/new inflation.
breaks: Inflation requires slow roll on a flat plateau, which is not generic for SSB potentials, and the inflaton has no established particle identity.

name: Homology and mass–luminosity scaling
summary: Dimensional and homology arguments give stellar scalings such as L∝M³ for radiative stars and the Eddington luminosity, together with the Chandrasekhar mass from fundamental constants.

name: Constraints on varying constants from the CMB
summary: A different fine-structure constant or electron mass at recombination shifts the recombination epoch and alters peak positions. Planck data and quasar absorption spectra bound such variation.

name: Cosmological constant problem across Planck scales
summary: Planck-unit estimates of the vacuum energy exceed the observed dark-energy density by about 120 orders of magnitude. The mismatch is the sharpest naturalness problem.

name: Stellarator optimization with differentiable and ML tools
summary: Stellarator coil and shape optimization uses adjoint or automatic differentiation and surrogate models over a large 3D parameter space.

name: Disruption prediction and plasma control with ML
summary: Tokamak disruption predictors and deep-RL magnetic controllers (e.g. on TCV) apply ML to real-time control where first-principles models are too slow.

name: ML surrogates and control in fusion
summary: Neural surrogates of gyrokinetic fluxes accelerate transport modelling, and reinforcement learning has been used for tokamak shape control and disruption prediction.

name: Ab initio MD for warm dense matter
summary: Warm dense matter equations of state and conductivities are computed by finite-temperature DFT-MD and path-integral Monte Carlo, bridging condensed matter methods to plasma conditions.

name: Strongly coupled plasmas studied by MD
summary: The one-component plasma and Yukawa systems are benchmark MD systems, with melting at Γ≈175 (OCP) and dusty-plasma crystals; MD gives transport and equation of state where perturbation theory fails.

name: Particle pushers and MD integrators
summary: PIC particle pushing and MD both integrate N-body trajectories with time-reversible Verlet-like schemes; MD with Coulomb forces uses Ewald or PPPM mesh methods also used in PIC.

name: Path-integral Monte Carlo for dense plasmas
summary: Fermionic PIMC and the sign problem constrain what can be computed for hydrogen and electron gases at WDM conditions; restricted and permutation-blocking variants give benchmark equations of state.

name: Monte Carlo neutronics and alpha-particle transport
summary: Neutron transport, tritium breeding and shielding in fusion devices use Monte Carlo codes, and Monte Carlo Fokker–Planck operators model fast-alpha slowing down.
